name: Fufu with light soup
subtitle: Fufu is a dough of boiled cassava pounded together with plantain, cocoyam or yam; it is a traditional food of the Akan peoples of Ghana, eaten throughout the country.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: A traditional food of the Akan peoples of Ghana, eaten by millions of other Ghanaians.

facts.label: Main ingredients
facts.value: A pounded dough of cooked cassava with plantain, cocoyam or yam.

facts.label: How it is made
facts.value: Traditionally prepared by hand by two or more people using a wooden mortar and pestle.

facts.label: How it is eaten
facts.value: Many young fufu eaters prefer light soup, made with pepper, onion and tomatoes.

facts.label: Change
facts.value: The first fufu pounding machine was developed in 2004 by a Ghanaian electrical-equipment dealer, Fadegnom Charles.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A combination of boiled cassava and boiled plantain pounded together into soft balls.

facts.label: How it is made
facts.value: One person pounds with a heavy stick while another turns the paste.

facts.label: How it is eaten
facts.value: Fufu is not chewed but tasted and then swallowed.

facts.label: Light soup
facts.value: Light soup may be made with goat or chicken and is served with fufu, banku or rice.

parts.text: Fufu is a dough of boiled cassava pounded together with plantain, cocoyam or yam; it is a traditional food of the Akan peoples of Ghana, eaten throughout the country. Light soup is a soup made with pepper, onion and tomatoes, often with goat or chicken. Fufu was long pounded by hand in a wooden mortar by two or more people; mechanical fufu pounders, the first built in 2004, are now widely used.
Fufu is served in soft balls with soup and is swallowed rather than chewed; many younger Ghanaians prefer it with light soup, while Asante tradition favours palm nut, kontomire or groundnut soup.
